---
title: "Calibration"
description: "The agreement between a model's predicted confidence and observed outcome frequencies."
term: "Calibration"
letter: "C"
category: "Model Evaluation"
difficulty: "Advanced"
---

## Simple explanation

A model is calibrated when predictions made with a particular confidence
are correct about as often as that confidence suggests. For example, among
many predictions assigned confidence 0.8, roughly 80% should be correct
for that event.

## Technical explanation

For a probabilistic classifier, calibration compares predicted
probabilities with empirical frequencies. A model can rank examples well
but be poorly calibrated. Reliability diagrams, the Brier score, and
expected calibration error are among the tools used to assess calibration,
each with limitations and sensitivity to binning or dataset size.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Confidence estimates may guide human review, triage, or automated
thresholds. Poor calibration can make downstream decisions unreliable,
even when classification accuracy is strong.

## How it works

Collect predictions and outcomes on data representative of the intended
use. Group predictions by confidence and compare each group's average
confidence with its observed accuracy. Calibration methods such as
temperature scaling can adjust probability estimates using held-out
calibration data.

## Practical example

If a classifier marks 100 validation examples as having an 80% chance of
belonging to a class, a calibrated model should be correct on approximately
80 of them over repeated comparable cases.

## Common misconceptions

- High accuracy does not imply good calibration.
- Calibration on one dataset or population may not transfer to another.
- A confidence score from a generative model is not automatically a
  calibrated probability of factual correctness.
